short: The siege that ended the Aztec empire and founded Spanish Mexico.
full:
Driven out of Tenochtitlan on the Noche Triste in June 1520, Hernan Cortes withdrew to Tlaxcala, rebuilt his force around tens of thousands of indigenous allies, and had thirteen brigantines built in sections and carried overland to Lake Texcoco. The siege began in late May 1521. The brigantines took control of the water, the causeways were cut one by one, and the aqueduct bringing fresh water from Chapultepec was severed.

The defenders under Cuauhtemoc fought street by street for some eleven weeks while smallpox and starvation did the rest; the Spanish demolished buildings as they advanced to deny cover. Cuauhtemoc was captured trying to escape by canoe and the city surrendered on 13 August 1521. The victory handed Spain the administrative machinery of a dense, tribute-paying state, which it took over largely intact. That inheritance, more than any battlefield advantage, is why a few hundred Europeans could govern millions.
